title: A Layered Taxonomy of AI-Driven Patient–Trial Matching: From Rules to Agents and the Evaluation-Validity Gap
content: Manually matching patients to complex clinical-trial eligibility criteria is a long-standing bottleneck in clinical research, and the AI systems built to address it have multiplied without a shared vocabulary for what they actually do. This perspective organizes that work as a stack of six interoperating capability layers, running from deterministic rule-based filtering up to agentic clinical workflows, rather than as a sequence of competing eras. Drawing on work published between 2015 and 2025 and anchored to the field’s shared benchmarks, the n2c2 cohort-selection task, the TREC Clinical Trials tracks, and the Chia corpus, it shows that the strongest current systems are hybrids: they retrieve, rerank, and then reason, as TrialGPT and RECTIFIER both do. Generative components handle complex logical and temporal criteria well, but they add latency and cost, and they can hallucinate in ways that complicate real use. The argument is that the binding constraint is shifting away from information extraction and toward trustworthy eligibility judgment when the ground truth itself is uncertain, a problem this paper terms the evaluation-validity gap. Six methodological gaps still separate prototypes from routine practice, and evaluation validity under weak or retrospective labels is arguably the most consequential of them. Closing it will depend more on rigorous evaluation, explanation, and fairness, and on the regulatory frameworks now taking shape inside the FDA, the EU, and several US states, than on building larger models.
